impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—which holds that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply to prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct, and whether a reference patent can claim the filing date of its provisional application without satisfying written description requirements for any claim.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's decision finding claims of the '409 patent unpatentable as obvious, remanding for reconsideration of whether the Carrier reference qualified as prior art under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court questioned the Board's Penumbra framework, which allowed a reference to receive its provisional filing date without a Dynamic Drinkware-style written description analysis. This decision has significant implications for how provisional application filing dates are used to establish prior art status in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially stricter standard for establishing prior art dates, making it harder for IPR petitioners to rely on provisional application dates of reference patents without proving written description support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty using references with provisional filing dates as prior art, potentially increasing the cost and uncertainty of patent challenges.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in a prior IPR petition but allegedly could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standard for applying § 315(e)(2) estoppel and warns against using hindsight to evaluate what a skilled searcher could have found. This ruling affects the scope of invalidity defenses available to accused infringers after IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions, as courts must apply a rigorous evidentiary standard before imposing estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in using IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity challenges, potentially increasing the cost and duration of patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, and affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. The case addresses the application of the Alice/Mayo framework to communication technology patents. The split outcome on eligibility across related patents provides important guidance on how § 101 applies to technical standards-related inventions.
impacts.positiveImplications: The affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and the denial of JMOL on damages validates patent enforcement in communications technology standards, supporting patent holders' ability to recover significant damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur of eligibility for other claims in the same patent family demonstrates continued uncertainty in § 101 eligibility determinations, creating litigation risk for both patent owners and implementers of technical standards.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in its judgment on trade secret misappropriation damages and breach of contract damages arising from a software licensing relationship.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's breach of contract judgment and reinstated the jury award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case provides significant guidance on trade secret damages methodology in complex software licensing disputes and the proper scope of Daubert exclusions for damages experts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret owners benefit from the court's willingness to allow broader damages models and its reinstatement of the breach of contract jury award, strengthening the enforcement value of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face continued exposure to trade secret misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government should be assessed by reference to existing license agreement terms or through a hypothetical negotiation, and what constitutes the proper application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in calculating damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation rather than existing license terms to assess copyright infringement damages but vacated the damages award in part, finding the court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This case establishes important principles for how copyright damages are calculated in government infringement cases involving commercially licensed software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies can pursue copyright infringement claims against the government using hypothetical negotiation methodology, which may yield different (potentially higher) damages than existing license rates.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur of portions of the damages award and the rejection of certain 'book of wisdom' applications may limit the ability to inflate damages based on post-infringement developments.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an alleged typographical error in a provisional patent application (changing 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent range) constituted new matter that broke the priority chain, thereby allowing an intervening public disclosure to anticipate the patent's claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the change from C2-C12-alkyl in the provisional application to C1-C12-alkyl in the non-provisional patent was not merely correcting an obvious typographical error and thus constituted new matter. Because the patent could not claim priority to its provisional application, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the patent's claims. This ruling has major implications for pharmaceutical patent priority and the treatment of typographical errors in patent applications.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from a strict standard for priority claims, making it harder for patent owners to retroactively correct errors in provisional applications to cover competitor products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies face significant risk that even minor errors in provisional applications may break priority chains and expose patents to intervening prior art, potentially invalidating valuable drug patents.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of the cancer drug cabozantinib (L)-malate satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of the Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description, upholding Exelixis's patents covering crystalline forms of the active ingredient in Cabometyx® cancer treatment. This decision reinforces the enforceability of pharmaceutical polymorph patents and supports brand-name drug companies' ability to maintain patent protection over specific salt forms used in commercial products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for crystalline form patents, strengthening protection for branded drug products against generic competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry where branded companies hold patents on specific crystalline forms, potentially delaying access to lower-cost alternatives.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a drug combination patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching its generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the bond requirement pending appeal. The claim construction ruling addressed whether the weight-to-weight ratio in the patent claim refers to the free base or salt forms of the active ingredients. This case has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent litigation involving drug combination patents and ANDA challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction blocking generic competition, preserving market exclusivity during the patent's remaining term.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur of the bond waiver means patent holders must post security when obtaining preliminary injunctions against generic competitors, potentially creating significant financial obligations if the injunction is later reversed.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether design patent claim construction involves factual questions that should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc on challenges to the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement. The divided court rejected arguments that the framework improperly focuses on differences rather than similarities and that claim construction in design patents involves jury questions. The concurrence defended the existing framework while dissenting judges argued for reconsideration. This decision maintains the current legal standard governing design patent infringement analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of design patent infringement benefit from the preservation of a framework that allows summary judgment based on visual differences, potentially reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders may face continued difficulty proving infringement at summary judgment under a framework that some judges view as overemphasizing differences, and the dissent signals potential future instability in the law.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities implicitly overruled Federal Circuit precedent in Bright v. United States on this issue.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe class action tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision. Bank holding company plaintiffs who lost significant assets during the 2008 financial crisis could not revive their takings and breach of contract claims after the limitations period expired. This ruling has broad implications for class action tolling in government claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors with claims against the federal government cannot rely on American Pipe tolling to extend the § 2501 limitations period, requiring more timely individual filings and reducing the ability to wait for class action outcomes before filing individual suits.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment provision, or whether such a contract interpretation dispute should be heard by the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a patent settlement agreement, finding the case turned on contract interpretation under state law rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent disputes and affects where companies litigate settlement agreement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies may benefit from having settlement agreement disputes heard in regional circuits that may have different procedural and substantive approaches than the Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements face jurisdictional uncertainty and potential forum-shopping concerns when disputes arise over contingent payment provisions, adding cost and delay.

impacts.caseName: Ridge Corp. v. Kirk NationaLease Co.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted a preliminary injunction for infringement of a patent directed to insulated overhead doors, including claims of tortious interference based on a patent counsel letter sent to a third-party manufacturer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the preliminary injunction granted against the KNL defendants for alleged infringement of the '084 patent covering insulated overhead doors. The case also involved a tortious interference claim based on a patent counsel letter asserting potential royalty liability to a third-party manufacturer. The reversal affects the standard for obtaining preliminary injunctions in patent cases and the interplay between patent enforcement letters and tortious interference claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of patent infringement benefit from a more rigorous standard for preliminary injunctions, reducing the risk of being enjoined before a full trial on the merits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty obtaining preliminary injunctive relief, and the case highlights risks associated with sending enforcement letters to third parties that may give rise to tortious interference counterclaims.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 as an exceptional case, and imposed sanctions on plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint alleging that Volkswagen infringed a patent on electrically controlled spectacles, the award of over $207,000 in attorney fees to Volkswagen as an exceptional case under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the proposed amended complaint was futile and the litigation was exceptional. This decision reinforces deterrents against frivolous patent infringement suits and counsel misconduct.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies facing meritless patent assertions have strong fee-shifting and sanctions tools to recover litigation costs and deter future frivolous filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial exposure for bringing claims that courts deem insufficiently supported, with both § 285 fees and § 1927 sanctions potentially imposing joint and several liability.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on any such deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade's decision that had declared Commerce's 15-day participation deadline regulation void and enjoined its enforcement. The court held that the statute is silent on when parties must indicate intent to participate, and Commerce's regulatory deadline was a permissible exercise of delegated authority. This decision is significant for antidumping enforcement and international trade, preserving Commerce's ability to set procedural deadlines in sunset reviews.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from preserved procedural rules that keep sunset reviews on track, helping maintain antidumping duty orders that protect against unfairly priced imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign manufacturers face continued strict procedural deadlines in sunset reviews, with the risk that failure to meet the 15-day deadline could result in adverse determinations.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of a patent directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL on both invalidity (anticipation) and non-infringement of the '296 patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions. The court's reversal of both liability findings eliminates a significant patent infringement judgment in the medical device space. This ruling affects the enforceability of university-owned biomedical patents against major device manufacturers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from a rigorous application of anticipation and non-infringement standards that can overturn adverse jury verdicts, reducing exposure to large patent damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent owners and licensees face the risk that appellate courts may reverse favorable jury verdicts on both invalidity and non-infringement grounds, undermining the value of their patent portfolios.
